items.title: Nadra launches locally made QR code-based identity cards
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) on Wednesday launched a new chipless National Identity Card (NIC) built around a secure QR code, replacing the imported microchip used for the past 14 years. The card has been manufactured domestically by the National Security Printing Company (NSPC) in Karachi in line with Nadra’s technical and security specifications, a statement issued by the authority on Friday said. Instead of a chip, the card will carry a secure QR code that can be scanned and verified on a smartphone through Nadra’s Pak Identity (PakID) mobile application, it added. The federal government approved the issuance of the new card on February 23 this year. The code will contain the cardholder’s information and photograph. According to Nadra, this will allow institutions to enter individuals’ names, addresses and other identity details more easily and consistently in their systems while reducing data entry errors. The card will also display a family number and symbols to denote persons with disabilities, senior citizens, organ donors and citizens of Azad Jammu and Kashmir. The cardholder’s name and address will be printed in both Urdu and English, Nadra added. The visible and covert security features of the card have been “updated to meet current requirements and align with domestic manufacturing capabilities”, the statement said. Nadra said the chip-based Smart NIC introduced about 14 years ago could not be fully utilised as chip readers and supporting infrastructure were never widely available. The QR-based card addresses this gap, being verifiable through an ordinary smartphone or software connected to a camera, it said. Telecom operators, banks, hospitals, the Pakistan Railways, police and other authorised institutions will also be provided with software to read and verify the QR code, Nadra said. The rollout will be phased, with the QR code-based card replacing the standard CNIC from Friday, it said, adding that from January 2027, it will be issued for all categories, including NICs for Overseas Pakistanis (Nicops) and Juvenile Cards. In the final phase, the Pakistan Origin Card (POC) will also transition to the chipless format, according to the statement. Nadra clarified that all previously issued identity cards would remain valid until their expiry dates. In February, the government notified amendments to the National Identity Card Rules, 2002 and the Pakistan Origin Card Rules, 2002 to modernise the country’s identity document framework. Part of these reforms included the statutory introduction of the QR code — a scannable barcode containing horizontal and vertical lines, dots, and patterns — as a defined security and verification feature. The amendments further authorised the use of a QR code or “any other technological feature”, in lieu of the current microchip, enabling Nadra to adopt evolving verification technologies without repeated rule amendments.

items.title: Les États-Unis veulent évaluer la loyauté de leurs alliés de l’OTAN
items.description: Washington a recemment envoye aux pays membres de l'OTAN un questionnaire visant a mesurer leur soutien a la politique de Donald Trump, sur fond de possible reduction de la presence militaire americaine en Europe. Selon un article de Bloomberg, qui a revele l'existence du document le 14 août, les allies doivent notamment preciser s'ils ont apporte un « soutien public » a la politique etrangere des etats-Unis et quelles restrictions ils ont imposees a l'utilisation de bases militaires par les forces americaines. Le document va au-dela des seules questions de securite. Washington veut egalement savoir si ses partenaires achetent des armes aupres d'entreprises americaines et s'ils soutiennent des regles susceptibles de limiter l'acces de ces societes aux contrats de defense europeens. Les pays sont aussi interroges sur leur position concernant le principe du « Made in Europe » dans le secteur de l'armement. Cette demarche intervient alors que l'administration Trump mene un reexamen de six mois de son dispositif militaire en Europe, dont les conclusions sont attendues en decembre. Dans le meme temps, Washington cherche a transferer une part croissante des responsabilites militaires et financieres aux membres europeens de l'Alliance. Des divergences de plus en plus visibles au sein de l'OTAN Les questions posees par Washington renvoient directement a plusieurs differends recents avec certains de ses allies. Celles concernant l'acces aux bases militaires portent notamment sur les operations americaines au Moyen-Orient et dans l'hemisphere occidental. L'Espagne avait ainsi refuse de soutenir les frappes americaines contre l'Iran et interdit l'utilisation de ses bases a cette fin. Le questionnaire fait egalement reference, de maniere indirecte, a l'Iran ainsi qu'a l'operation americaine visant Nicolás Maduro au Venezuela. Ces episodes illustrent les divergences qui peuvent apparaître lorsque certains membres de l'Alliance refusent de suivre automatiquement les initiatives de Washington. La demarche a d'ailleurs ete mal accueillie par plusieurs pays de l'OTAN. D'apres les sources citees par Bloomberg, certains allies y voient une tentative de les pousser vers un alignement politique et ideologique en echange du maintien des garanties de securite americaines. L'agence estime qu'une telle evolution pourrait modifier sensiblement l'equilibre des relations transatlantiques herite de l'apres-guerre. Washington reduit progressivement son role militaire en Europe Le questionnaire s'inscrit dans une revision plus large de la presence americaine sur le continent. Le 28 juillet, le responsable du Pentagone Elbridge Colby avait confirme le lancement de cet examen, en soulignant que l'administration Trump entendait transferer davantage de responsabilites militaires aux allies europeens. La reduction des effectifs americains avait deja ete evoquee au printemps. Donald Trump avait alors annonce de nouvelles diminutions de la presence militaire des etats-Unis en Europe, au-dela du retrait deja prevu de 5 000 militaires d'Allemagne. La legislation americaine interdit toutefois une baisse des effectifs sous le seuil de 76 000 militaires en Europe sans justification supplementaire. L'ampleur et la repartition d'un eventuel retrait restent donc a determiner. Le secretaire general de l'OTAN, Mark Rutte, a qualifie le reexamen americain de decision « logique et positive », compte tenu de la hausse des depenses militaires europeennes et canadiennes. Un representant de l'Alliance a egalement confirme a Bloomberg que des discussions etaient en cours avec Washington, sans commenter directement le questionnaire. Les decisions attendues d'ici la fin de l'annee devraient ainsi preciser jusqu'ou les etats-Unis comptent reduire leur presence militaire directe en Europe. Elles permettront egalement de voir dans quelle mesure Washington entend desormais conditionner davantage son engagement aupres de ses allies a leur alignement politique, a leurs choix militaires et a leurs achats dans le secteur de la defense.

items.title: 2 suspects in fatal attacks on Lahore cops killed in Muridke fire exchange, say police
items.description: LAHORE: Two men who allegedly shot dead three police officials in Lahore on Thursday were killed during an exchange of fire with law enforcers at a house in Muridke where they had held a family hostage, police sources told Dawn . Police officials identified the suspects as a father-son duo, Fayyaz Butt and Rehan Butt, saying that they were killed in a joint operation by Lahore police, Counter-Terrrorism Department (CTD) personnel, Sheikhpura police and Elite Force personnel on Friday morning after an hours-long chase from Lahore to Muridke. The suspects held the driver of a Lahore Waste Management Company vehicle at gunpoint and forced him to keep on driving to reach Muridke, the officials said. According to police, they allegedly shot dead two policemen in Lahore’s Badami Bagh area and one at Yateem Khana Chowk, Multan Road, besides injuring three on Thursday night. Initial police inquiries showed that the first armed attack was carried out by Rehan and his accomplices in Badami Bagh. The martyred officials were identified as Sub-Inspector (SI) Adeel Ashiq and Constable Asad. An hour later, the suspects allegedly targeted policemen deployed at the headquarters of the banned Tehreek-i-Labbaik Pakistan (TLP) on Multan Road and opened indiscriminate firing. On Friday, a senior official who coordinated the joint operation against the suspects told Dawn a third suspect, identified as Tariq, managed to flee. His last location was reported as Bagh in Azad Jammu Kashmir (AJK). AJK police and the law enforcement agencies from Punjab were working to trace and arrest him, he said. Regarding Friday’s operation, the official said Fayyaz and Rehan were traced to a seminary in Muridke. Law enforcers surrounded it after reaching the site while the seminary’s management claimed that the two were not present there. To verify the claim, police seized the seminary’s DVR, but found that the cameras were not working, he said, adding that the DVR was sent to Lahore for forensic analysis. Meanwhile, law enforcers received information that the suspects had gone toward River Ravi and were hiding in a forest, the official said. On the directions of IG police Punjab Abdul Kareem, the police used thermal drones to trace the suspects in the forest, he said, adding that the suspects moved to a densely populated area as they realised they were being traced. “They barged into a house, took the family hostage and threatened to kill them,” he said, adding that the suspects opened fire on the police personnel when they reached there. During the exchange of fire, Rehan and Fayyaz were killed, he said. He said Tariq had separated from them and fled to AJK during the chase. After Thursday’s attack, a police official had told Dawn that the incidents seemed to be an act of revenge. Rehan’s brother, Faizan Butt, was allegedly killed in an encounter with a CTD team, which reportedly included SI Adeel, a few years back, the official said. Faizan was reportedly working for the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and he was involved in the killing of some police officials, the police official said. He added that SI Adeel had told police higher-ups in 2024 that he was receiving life threats from Rehan. Following his complaint, a first information report was registered against Rehan in November 2024 with Shafiqabad police. According to the FIR, Adeel had alleged that he had received a WhatsApp call from Rehan, who had threatened to kill him.

items.title: La Tunisie et la Libye lancent un vaste appel d’offres conjoint pour l’exploration pétrolière et gazière en Méditerranée
items.description: La Tunisie et la Libye relancent leur appel d'offres petrolier et gazier dans le bassin offshore de Gabes-Tripoli, avec une ouverture prevue le 7 septembre 2026. Pilotee par la societe commune Joint Oil, la procedure porte sur deux volets : l'exploration d'un bloc de 3 000 km² et le developpement du gisement transfrontalier de Zarat. Creee en 1988, Joint Oil gere les ressources de cette zone maritime commune aux deux pays. L'appel d'offres restera ouvert jusqu'au 31 decembre 2026. Les compagnies disposant d'une experience confirmee dans l'exploration et le developpement offshore pourront acceder a une salle de donnees virtuelle geree par le cabinet Moyes & Co. Les candidats retenus seront informes le 26 fevrier 2027, avant les attributions officielles prevues d'ici au 30 avril 2027. Joint Oil presentera egalement les projets a Londres, le 9 septembre 2026 lors du Mediterranean, Middle East & Africa Scout Group, puis les 29 et 30 septembre au World Energy Summit. Un bassin offshore a fort potentiel Le volet exploration concerne une zone situee dans des eaux de 80 a 120 metres de profondeur. Le bloc est deja couvert par environ 1 900 km² de donnees sismiques 3D, auxquels s'ajoutent 6 500 km de profils sismiques 2D. Il dispose egalement des resultats de cinq puits d'exploration fores entre 1976 et 2010. Cinq principales cibles ont ete identifiees : Faisal, Hadaf, Siraj Est, Siraj Ouest et Zarat profond. Leurs ressources moyennes en place depasseraient 1,6 milliard de barils de petrole et 87,8 milliards de m³ de gaz naturel. Hadaf concentre le potentiel petrolier le plus important, avec un peu plus d'un milliard de barils estimes en place. Siraj Ouest apparaît comme la principale cible gaziere, avec environ 48,1 milliards de m³ de gaz, auxquels s'ajouteraient 358 millions de barils de petrole. Le bloc se trouve par ailleurs a proximite de plusieurs champs deja exploites, notamment Bouri, Al Jurf et Bahr Essalam cote libyen, ainsi qu'Ashtart, Miskar et Didon cote tunisien. Cette proximite avec des installations existantes pourrait faciliter le developpement d'eventuelles decouvertes et leur integration aux infrastructures energetiques regionales. Zarat, un projet commun au cœur du developpement a ce programme d'exploration s'ajoute un projet plus avance : le developpement de Zarat. Decouvert par Marathon Oil en 1992, le gisement est situe a cheval sur la frontiere maritime tuniso-libyenne. Zarat contiendrait 266 millions de barils de petrole et de condensats ainsi que 31,1 milliards de m³ de gaz en place. Les reserves recuperables sont estimees a 72 millions de barils et 23,6 milliards de m³ de gaz. Sa mise en valeur necessitera plusieurs accords entre la Tunisie et la Libye, notamment sur le partage de la production, l'unification des ressources et l'exploitation commune du gisement. Parmi les solutions envisagees figurent le raccordement de plusieurs puits a une unite de production offshore et l'utilisation des infrastructures regionales pour l'evacuation du petrole. Avec cette relance, Tunis et Tripoli cherchent ainsi a mieux valoriser leurs ressources offshore communes et a approfondir une cooperation energetique bilaterale engagee depuis plusieurs decennies. Le projet s'inscrit ainsi dans une logique de developpement conjoint d'un bassin partage, reposant directement sur les interets et les capacites des deux pays voisins.

items.title: Saisies de navires russes : Londres s'inquiète du manque de moyens pour faire face à Moscou
items.description: Le Royaume-Uni ne disposerait pas d'une puissance de feu suffisante pour empecher la Russie de s'emparer de navires britanniques dans l'hypothese d'une confrontation de ce type, rapporte le 13 août le Telegraph , citant plusieurs sources du secteur de la defense. Selon les interlocuteurs du quotidien, les inquietudes portent principalement sur l'Indo-Pacifique, ou la presence militaire britannique est jugee trop limitee pour faire face a une eventuelle saisie de bâtiments par la Russie. Cette situation est notamment attribuee a la reduction progressive des moyens de la Royal Navy . L'ancien chef de la marine britannique, l'amiral Alan West, a vivement critique cette evolution, estimant que les gouvernements successifs avaient laisse la flotte diminuer au point qu'elle ne dispose desormais plus d'un nombre suffisant de navires pour remplir sa mission de protection de la navigation mondiale. Dans l'ocean Indien, la marine britannique ne dispose actuellement que de deux patrouilleurs susceptibles d'assurer la protection de navires du Royaume-Uni : le HMS Tamar et le HMS Spey, tous deux faiblement armes. Pour Alan West, ces bâtiments servent avant tout a assurer une presence britannique dans la region. Il a rappele qu'il y a encore une trentaine d'annees, quatre ou cinq navires y etaient deployes, contre seulement deux aujourd'hui. Face a cette faiblesse des moyens disponibles, l'ancien ministre britannique de la Defense, Ben Wallace, a suggere de s'appuyer davantage sur les allies. Il a notamment evoque la possibilite de solliciter la France afin de mieux repartir les missions a l'echelle mondiale, notamment pour assurer des fonctions d'escorte ou de protection. Le 12 août, le president russe Vladimir Poutine a prevenu que Moscou repondrait de maniere symetrique si des pays occidentaux procedaient a la saisie de navires russes. « Ils ont pense qu'il etait possible de saisir nos navires et de vendre les biens voles. Il s'agit, bien sûr, de piraterie et de vol. Et si cela se concretise, nous serons contraints de repondre de facon symetrique. Et pas necessairement dans les eaux ou ils prevoient d'attaquer nos navires. Mais la ou nous le jugerons approprie. N'importe ou. Y compris dans la zone de responsabilite de la flotte du Pacifique », a-t-il fait savoir. Le vice-president du Conseil de securite russe, Dmitri Medvedev , a ensuite developpe cette position. Invoquant le principe de reciprocite, il a affirme que la Russie pourrait prendre pour cible tout navire marchand se trouvant dans ses eaux ou dans des eaux neutres si elle avait suffisamment de raisons de soupconner que celui-ci transporte une cargaison destinee aux interets de l'adversaire.

items.title: Boké : le Consortium SMB-Winning lance une formation de deux mois pour 73 jeunes
items.description: Face aux exigences technologiques et opérationnelles des métiers d’aujourd’hui, la qualification professionnelle constitue un véritable levier pour renforcer l’employabilité des jeunes. C’est dans ce cadre que la direction générale du Consortium SMB-Winning a lancé, ce vendredi 14 août 2026, à l’École régionale des arts et métiers (ERAM) de Boké, un programme de formation professionnelle destiné à 73 jeunes issus des communautés impactées des préfectures de Boké et de Télimélé. D’une durée de deux mois, cette formation vise principalement à doter les bénéficiaires de compétences adaptées aux besoins réels du marché de l’emploi et aux exigences des secteurs minier, industriel et artisanal. Pour le premier vice-maire de la commune urbaine de Boké, Abdoulaye Manè, cette initiative illustre l’engagement des entreprises minières, notamment la SMB, en faveur de leur responsabilité sociétale. Il a salué les efforts consentis pour renforcer les compétences des jeunes et mieux les préparer à leur avenir professionnel. Au nom du Collège des techniciens et professionnels des métiers (CPTM), Boubacar Kanté a rappelé que cette cérémonie marque le début d’un parcours de formation de deux mois pour les jeunes de Boké et de Télimélé. Il a particulièrement insisté sur l’importance de la qualification professionnelle des jeunes dans les différents domaines de compétence. Il a également salué l’engagement du Consortium SMB-Winning dans la valorisation de la jeunesse et l’adaptation de ses compétences aux exigences du marché de l’emploi, une démarche qui, selon lui, s’inscrit dans la vision du président Mamadi Doumbouya à travers le programme Simandou 2040. De son côté, le directeur général du département des relations communautaires du Consortium SMB-Winning et coordinateur du projet Simandou, Wu Kiong, a déclaré que cette session de formation constitue une nouvelle étape importante dans la concrétisation des engagements de la SMB en matière de responsabilité sociétale, de promotion du contenu local et d’accompagnement durable des communautés riveraines de ses zones d’opération. Il a souligné que le développement durable d’une région repose notamment sur la valorisation de son capital humain, la formation professionnelle de sa jeunesse et la création d’opportunités concrètes d’insertion socioprofessionnelle. Selon lui, la présence du Consortium SMB-Winning s’inscrit également dans une vision à long terme visant à bâtir un partenariat solide, responsable et mutuellement bénéfique avec les communautés. « Chers jeunes de Boké et Télimélé, l’opportunité qui vous est offerte aujourd’hui est le fruit d’un partenariat ambitieux. Mais sa réussite dépendra de votre engagement et de votre détermination », a-t-il lancé aux bénéficiaires. En ouvrant officiellement les travaux de cette session de formation destinée aux 73 jeunes de Boké et de Télimélé, le secrétaire général de la préfecture de Boké, Sékouba Traoré, a estimé que cette initiative témoigne de la volonté du Consortium SMB-Winning de « construire la Guinée avec les Guinéens ». Il a également cité plusieurs réalisations et initiatives communautaires du Consortium SMB-Winning, notamment la construction d’une ligne ferroviaire de 135 kilomètres, le lancement des travaux de construction de la route reliant Boké à Télimélé ainsi que la formation professionnelle de 73 jeunes des deux préfectures. Pour le représentant de l’administration préfectorale, la formation de la jeunesse constitue un investissement essentiel pour l’avenir. « Former la jeunesse, c’est tourner les pages d’un passé sombre marqué par les manifestations de rue, les perturbations des activités minières et les grèves illimitées », a-t-il déclaré. Cette nouvelle initiative du Consortium SMB-Winning entend ainsi contribuer au renforcement des compétences locales et favoriser une meilleure insertion des jeunes des communautés riveraines dans le tissu économique et professionnel de la région.

items.title: Burkina: Une centaine d’enfants initiés aux valeurs du sport et de la discipline par la gendarmerie
items.description: BURKINA-SPORT-SECURITE-CAMP-VACANCES Burkina: Une centaine d’enfants initiés aux valeurs du sport et de la discipline par la gendarmerie Ouagadougou, 14 août 2026 (AIB)- La Gendarmerie nationale a clôturé vendredi, la première édition du camp vacances football, qui a permis d’inculquer à une centaine d’enfants les valeurs de discipline, de respect et d’esprit d’équipe durant un mois, afin de faire d’eux les futurs bâtisseurs du Burkina Faso. « Au-delà de la pratique du football, nous voulions offrir aux enfants un espace d’éducation, de loisirs sains et d’épanouissement, où le sport devient un véritable outil de formation humaine. Notre conviction est qu’investir dans l’enfant aujourd’hui, c’est investir dans l’homme et dans la nation de demain », a déclaré le promoteur, l’adjudant-chef Herman Zabsonré. Il a également expliqué qu’au-delà des performances sportives, il a constaté la naissance de nouvelles amitiés, le développement de l’esprit d’équipe et une meilleure compréhension des valeurs citoyennes. L’adjudant-chef Zabsonré a, par ailleurs, ajouté que les séances de sensibilisation ont permis aux enfants d’acquérir des outils leur permettant de promouvoir la paix autour d’eux. « Au regard des activités réalisées, nous pouvons affirmer avec satisfaction que les objectifs poursuivis ont été atteints. Les enfants ont renforcé leurs connaissances techniques et tactiques en football. Ils ont appris à jouer collectivement, à respecter les règles, à faire preuve de fair-play et à accepter aussi bien la victoire que la défaite avec dignité », a-t-il soutenu. Selon le parrain de la cérémonie, Mahamadou Sawadogo, le football enseigne la discipline, le respect, l’esprit d’équipe et le sens de l’effort. Il s’est dit convaincu que les connaissances acquises sur le terrain contribueront à faire des enfants de futurs citoyens engagés pour leur pays. « Nous avons surtout appris que le véritable champion est celui qui respecte ses adversaires, écoute ses éducateurs, encourage ses coéquipiers et fait preuve de discipline », a déclaré le représentant des participants, Nolan Sawadogo. Il a assuré que les différentes séances de sensibilisation leur ont permis de mieux comprendre l’importance du civisme, du patriotisme, du respect des symboles de leur pays, de la solidarité et du vivre-ensemble. « Ils repartent convaincus que chacun d’eux peut contribuer, à son niveau, à construire un Burkina Faso uni, paisible et prospère », a-t-il confié. Le promoteur a enfin appelé les participants à devenir des ambassadeurs des valeurs qu’ils ont apprises et à faire rayonner autour d’eux le respect, la solidarité, le patriotisme, la paix et la cohésion sociale. Agence d’information du Burkina LID/no/yos

items.title: Mali: le Premier ministre reçoit le Secrétaire général adjoint des Nations Unies, Haoliang Xu
items.description: Le Premier ministre, le Général de Division Abdoulaye Maïga a reçu ce vendredi 14 août 2026, au nom de Son Excellence le Général d’Armée Assimi Goïta, Président de la Transition, Chef de l’État, le Secrétaire général adjoint des Nations Unies et Administrateur adjoint du Programme des Nations Unies pour le développement (PNUD), Haoliang Xu. Dans le cadre de sa tournée sahélienne, il est en visite à Bamako dans le but de renforcer la coopération dans les domaines de l’économie, de l’administration territoriale et de la réconciliation. Pour l’hôte du jour, il s’agit de recueillir les réels défis du pays afin de mieux calibrer les apports, d'impulser la dynamique de développement basée sur les priorités nationales, ainsi que de consolider les acquis. Il s’est réjoui de la bonne articulation des priorités de développement, notamment dans le document de la Vision « MALI KURA ƝƐTAASIRA KA BƐN SAN 2063 MA », ainsi que la Stratégie Nationale pour l'Emergence et le Développement Durable (SNEDD) 2024-2033. En réponse, le Premier ministre a exprimé sa satisfaction pour l’accompagnement dont le Mali bénéficie de la part du PNUD et l’engagement du programme à respecter les principes qui guident l’action publique. Le Premier ministre a rappelé que le Mali entend rester cohérent face à la mise en œuvre efficiente de sa vision qui, a-t-il ajouté, concorde parfaitement avec les objectifs de développement durable du PNUD. Au titre des attentes, il a préconisé une approche onusienne basée sur les particularités et les singularités des États qui font face aux défis sécuritaires, afin d’adapter les interventions aux dimensions environnementale, économique et sociale. Le Chef du gouvernement a également réitéré l’ouverture du Mali à bénéficier davantage de l’accompagnement et de l’expertise du Programme des Nations Unies pour le développement. Source: CCRP-Primature L’article Mali: le Premier ministre reçoit le Secrétaire général adjoint des Nations Unies, Haoliang Xu est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: A Bleak, Violent Novel’s Unexpected Delights
items.description: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. Before his latest book, Marlon James hadn’t written a novel set in Jamaica in more than a decade. In the years following his Booker Prize–winning A Brief History of Seven Killings , the author focused on his Dark Star Trilogy , set in a fantasy universe. But after that long literary detour, he returned to the land of his birth in his new novel, The Disappearers —which is set primarily in Kingston and follows a group of characters, all queer Jamaican men, who meet while rehearsing a play that will never be seen. First, here are four new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: Hard-luck men in hardscrabble towns “Disunion,” a short story by Kurt Andersen A deeply layered novel about masculinity “Stance,” a poem by Deborah Garrison For this group, which gathers in secret in 1988, seeing and being seen are matters of life and death. The Kingston they inhabit is murderously homophobic, and accordingly, the novel can be quite bleak. But The Disappearers offers some delights too. Recently, in her article about the book for The Atlantic , Stephanie Burt noted that “the novel opens up many pleasures for literary readers,” who may recognize the numerous titles and references sprinkled throughout. I was deeply affected by how, almost universally, the characters seek out anything that proves that gay life exists on a larger scale. Lowbrow works, such as porn films and magazines, are most accessible; Playgirl and Hustler are name-checked. The songs of Boy George, Sylvester, and Prince are lifelines—the homoerotic cover of Prince’s 1988 album, Lovesexy , is an especially powerful beacon. Many of the characters are well read, and they name-drop gay novels such as Andrew Holleran’s Dancer From the Dance and E. M. Forster’s Maurice . For one of the men in particular, the type of hustling, defiant gay life that John Rechy describes in his nonfiction book The Sexual Outlaw is pivotal. The play they put on, a 1967 drama called Fortune and Men’s Eyes , explores homosexuality among a group of prisoners. Some of its characters see sex as a means for gaining or establishing power; others, as a convenient way to access pleasure. Some are what a modern audience might recognize as gay, whereas others choose partners largely because of their proximity. The cast share the characters’ disparate attitudes toward queerness. But in the Jamaica they live in, there is no room for nuance; any man seen as homosexual is a target for violence. Brutality will soon come to the rehearsal room. In a way, James has written a gay novel about the uses of a gay novel. When his characters invoke Oscar Wilde and Edmund White, Hadrian and Michelangelo, they’re proving, to themselves and to the reader, that queer life existed long before they came around. But James is not an unskeptical cheerleader for the healing power of visibility and representation. The Disappearers ’ major theme, after all, is that being recognized can be a bad thing: Owning these books is a hazard. Buying Lovesexy as a man in 1988 Kingston invites vigilantism. Staging Fortune and Men’s Eyes puts its cast and crew in danger. So why try to do it? The director and ringleader, Havelock Titus, asks himself this question more than a decade after those hopeful rehearsals. He knew, even at the time, that the effort was a risk. He still doesn’t know “what success would have meant,” because the unstaged play “never had the chance to become a failure.” But Havelock knows on some level that he did it because, just like those who came before him, he wanted to create some kind of evidence that gay men communed and survived in his time and place. In short, he was tired of being erased. Illustration by Roche Marlon James Returns to Realism, and to Jamaica By Stephanie Burt In his new novel, gay men struggle to escape violence in Kingston. Read the full article. What to Read The Age of Reform , by Richard Hofstadter History can’t fully explain the present or predict the future, but it can help us understand the patterns of contemporary politics and the likely paths ahead. In 1955, Hofstadter, one of the great American historians of the 20th century, published The Age of Reform —a political and social history of the years 1890 to 1940, the period of populism, progressivism, and the New Deal. Rapid technological change, monopoly power, deep inequality, endemic corruption, mass immigration, nativist demagogues, the transformation of both political parties, repeated efforts at reform, recurring spasms of reaction: Perhaps no other age so resembles our own. Hofstadter is brilliant at analyzing types that feel quite familiar to us today—the crusading urban progressive, the small-town conspiracy theorist. He was a liberal who sympathized with the passion for progress while unsentimentally diagnosing its illiberal ideas and motives. The fevered moralism of that age seems a long way from the paralyzing cynicism of ours. But reading Hofstadter will remind you that reform and reaction not only follow each other, but also often coexist in the same moment; neither ever has the last word. Americans are always dreaming of a better country, and some have actually made it so. — George Packer From our list: What’s the one book that explains American politics today? Out Next Week 📚 Finding Renée Richards , by Julie Kliegman 📚 The Jackal: The Rise and Fall of Carlos, the World’s First Super-Terrorist , by Joby Warrick 📚 The Book of Chuck , by LaToya Watkins Your Weekend Read Illustration by Ben Hickey Bring Back the Blue-Book Exam By Walt Hunter Universities find themselves in a surprising position. The only reliable way to evaluate what students have learned may be to bring back pen and paper. Faculty are reverting to in-person, handwritten assignments and timed essays—anything that keeps assessments offline. The unlikely hero of the day is the blue book, sales of which are up by as much as 80 percent for some universities since 2023. Read the full article. items.title: Sudan Nashra: In cross-border offensive, RSF seizes Blue Nile’s Geisan, recaptures Kurmuk | Military repels major RSF attack on North Kordofan’s Gabra al-Sheikh | After clashes inside Kauda, SPLM-N-Otoro fighting spreads to nearby villages | Kordofan governor in RSF-led govt defects | Back-to-back Sudanese visits to Juba in mutual push to contain border, Abyei tensions
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . The Rapid Support Forces and its allies launched a broad offensive across Sudan this week, opening simultaneous attacks on multiple fronts in what military officers described to Mada Masr as an attempt to offset heavy losses on the North Kordofan front and prevent military advances westward. From an attempt to retake a strategic border area in Darfur to waves of drone strikes across northern and central Sudan that kept the military’s air defenses heavily engaged, the escalation culminated with major gains in Blue Nile. The RSF and its ally the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, seized Geisan on Tuesday and retook Kurmuk two days later, advancing from SPLM-N-held territory in southern Blue Nile and across the Ethiopian border, three military sources told Mada Masr. The gains reverse much of the military’s recent progress along the southeastern border, coming only weeks after it recaptured Kurmuk and disrupted the cross-border supply routes that had sustained the allies’ campaign in the region. As the two sides were fighting in Kurmuk, an RSF force of more than 250 combat vehicles moved on Gabra al-Sheikh, one of the paramilitary group’s main logistics hub in North Kordofan, in an attempt to retake the area it lost in the military’s late-July offensive. The military and allied forces repelled the attack after several hours of fighting. While the SPLM-N remains occupied on the Blue Nile front, an internal crisis is growing in its South Kordofan stronghold, a crisis that could, a former military source in the movement said, force it to divert forces and resources to protecting its own territory from its own people. Clashes that broke out last week in Kauda, the movement’s seat of power, between SPLM-N forces and one of its oldest constituencies, the Otoro tribe, were brought under control within days. But this week, the confrontation spread to villages surrounding the town, where clashes and heavy artillery exchanges have driven a new wave of displacement. SPLM-N has since deployed heavily around Kauda to prevent the fighting from reaching the town again, a buildup that has disrupted people’s daily lives and deepened the strain on communities already exhausted by months of intermittent clashes and tightening security measures, three residents told Mada Masr. At the root of the latest violence are Otoro demands for greater representation in the movement’s civilian and military institutions — a pushback against what they see as an increasingly centralized mode of governance. Tribal notables in SPLM-N territory warn that without genuine outreach to local communities, the violence will keep recurring, testing the movement’s claim to offer a model of local governance distinct from central state rule and risking a deeper rift between its institutions and the people they govern. The RSF-led government is facing its own internal fractures. A fourth high-profile defection hit the administrative structures it has built in western Sudan, with Hamad Khalifa, the governor of the Kordofan region in the RSF-led Tasis administration and a member of its presidential council, announcing Wednesday that he is exiting the group. In the military-led government, Khartoum is accelerating its push for a domestic political track, targeting September for the launch of the intra-Sudanese dialogue Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has spent months championing and preparing — a process he wants to use to rebuild state institutions and set the terms for the next phase of the country’s political order under state oversight. The push picked up pace after international mediation in Addis Ababa broke down in late July, giving the government an opening to move ahead with its own track inside the country, a political source informed of the process said. The government is now working to settle the dialogue’s preparatory arrangements, from the composition of the committee that will organize it to the rules for participation and the issues to be addressed first. But those arrangements are themselves a source of contention, with the opposition Sumud coalition arguing that the forces expected to take part should have a say in shaping them, given that they will effectively determine the course of the process and its outcomes. Khartoum is also working with Juba through security talks to build direct channels between the two countries’ military and security agencies, as both sides seek to contain tensions along their shared border, Sudanese and South Sudanese sources told Mada Masr. A month of high-level contacts between the two capitals continued this week with back-to-back visits to Juba by Sudan’s Defense Minister Hassan Kabron and Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi. Talks focused on preventing armed groups and military supplies from crossing the border, protecting oil infrastructure crucial to both economies and managing tensions around the disputed Abyei area, after South Sudan decided to include it as an electoral district in its first general elections scheduled in December. *** In cross-border offensive, RSF seizes Blue Nile’s Geisan, recaptures Kurmuk RSF fighters and their allies, the SPLM-N (Hilu) forces led by Joseph Toka, attack the town of Geisan in Blue Nile state, August 11. Courtesy: Sudan War Monitor The RSF and its ally the SPLM-N have rapidly reversed the military’s recent gains in southeastern Blue Nile, seizing Geisan on Tuesday and retaking Kurmuk days later in an offensive launched from SPLM-N-held territory and across the Ethiopian border, three military sources told Mada Masr. The offensive has brought the two sides back into a fight over the state’s most strategically important border positions, only weeks after the military recaptured Kurmuk. The key cross-border gateway had fallen to the RSF and SPLM-N in March after the allies moved into Blue Nile from Ethiopia, opening a route for supplies and military support to reach their forces. The military’s July advance had put it on course to regain control of the southeastern border and disrupt the supply routes that had sustained its rivals’ campaign. Geisan appears to have then emerged as a major objective for the RSF and its allies. Its location near the Ethiopian border makes it strategically important as an alternative corridor for movement and supplies. The RSF-SPLM-N alliance began mobilizing for an offensive on Geisan shortly after losing Kurmuk in July. For a former military officer, the offensive in Blue Nile is a bid by the RSF to secure a compensatory victory after its heavy defeats on the Kordofan front and the military’s takeover of the Khartoum-Kordofan Saderat Road. According to the former officer, the group is also seeking to open a new front along the border that could stretch the military’s forces and disrupt its plans to expand westward toward Darfur. The offensive was prepared from across the border, according to the military sources. After withdrawing from Kurmuk in July , the RSF regrouped at camps in Asosa, in Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region, which borders Sudan, a military source said. The fighters were reinforced with additional personnel, including mercenaries of various nationalities who had undergone advanced military training in recent weeks ahead of the assault on Geisan, the source added. RSF fighters and their allies attacked Geisan in the early hours of Tuesday from two main axes, from the south and east, a second military source told Mada Masr. The assault was launched from inside Ethiopian territory and was accompanied by heavy drone strikes targeting military defenses and several key sites in the town, the source said. By Tuesday evening, the RSF had fully taken control of Geisan, after the military withdrew to Bakori, about 20 km from Damazin, where it maintains a large garrison, the source said. New troops have since arrived from Damazin to reinforce the area and reorganize ahead of a counteroffensive to retake Geisan, they added. The RSF-led Tasis alliance announced on the same day that it secured control of Geisan and inflicted heavy losses on the military in personnel and equipment. In a statement, the alliance said it seized all military positions in the town, along with large quantities of weapons and military equipment. Geisan’s importance stems not only from its location on the Ethiopian border, but also its wider strategic position in Blue Nile State. The town lies about 75 km southeast of the state capital Damazin and around 65 km from Roseires Dam, which supplies electricity to large parts of Sudan and provides irrigation for major agricultural schemes. From Geisan, the offensive then turned toward Kurmuk. Over the following days, strategic and suicide drones, along with heavy artillery fire launched from Ethiopian territory, pummeled Kurmuk, according to a third military source and a statement from the Kurmuk administration. On Thursday, the RSF and its allies moved on Kurmuk, attacking from three directions: from their new positions in Geisan to the northeast, from Ethiopian territory to the east and from the south, through areas controlled by the SPLM-N faction led by Joseph Toka, the military source said. The military withdrew toward Sali, north of Kurmuk, while its air force continued striking RSF positions inside the town, the source said. A local administrator in Asosa told Mada Masr that heavy infantry units were observed moving from an RSF base inside Ethiopia toward the border with Blue Nile state prior to Thursday’s attack. The official said he saw waves of military vehicles mounted with artillery moving toward the border, as well as soldiers wearing RSF uniforms. More than 20 civilians were killed in Geisan’s clashes on Tuesday, according to the UN. The International Organization for Migration said it recorded the displacement of around 2,500 people from Geisan to other locations within the locality. Others crossed into Ethiopia. The Geisan locality administration described the RSF attack as a “fully fledged crime” targeting residents’ livelihoods and security, particularly as they were busy cultivating their land for the agricultural season critical for food security. The third military source suggested that the RSF forces and its ally are unlikely to advance much farther, given the difficult terrain and the onset of heavy rains, which severely restrict the movement of personnel and vehicles. The military is expected to rely primarily on aerial attacks to wear down the RSF before launching any ground operation to retake Kurmuk, the source added. The former officer warned that Addis Ababa’s continued hosting of RSF training camps and launch points used to stage operations inside Sudan carries a regional risk under current circumstances — with Sudanese-Ethiopian relations already strained, and Ethiopia itself facing renewed instability in Tigray. Fighting broke out in early August between federal forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front in Western Tigray, which borders Sudan. If Khartoum responded in kind to Ethiopian support for the RSF, the former officer said, the confrontation could trigger a broader regional crisis. *** RSF launches simultaneous drone attacks on four cities The RSF launched a wave of suicide drone attacks on four cities in northern and central Sudan on Wednesday morning. Military ground defenses intercepted some of the drones before they reached their intended targets, according to three eyewitnesses who spoke to Mada Masr. In River Nile State, more than 20 RSF suicide drones targeting the cities of Damer and Atbara were shot down by military air defenses around the time of the dawn call to prayer, an eyewitness told Mada Masr. Explosions were heard until 6 am, the witness said. In Khartoum, an eyewitness in Bahri said RSF drones targeted civilian and military sites in northern and western Omdurman, as well as several locations in Bahri’s Doroshab area, including a mosque and a power station. Some of the drones were intercepted by air defenses, the witness said, and there were no casualties. In North Kordofan’s Obeid, several drones targeted the city, with one striking an area near a grocery store and a bank, killing a woman who had gone to the bank to collect her monthly pension and an employee of the judicial authority, an eyewitness said. The strikes led authorities to suspend work at several public facilities, close several schools and shut down Obeid’s main market. RSF drones returned to Omdurman on Thursday, an official in the city told Mada Masr, but no casualties were reported. *** New RSF attack on West Darfur’s Bir Saliba repelled The military-allied joint force repels an RSF attack on Bir Saliba in West Darfur, August 8. Courtesy: @AbedaMoham6183 on X The RSF launched a new attack on Bir Saliba in West Darfur on Saturday but was repelled by the military-allied joint force of armed movements, the latest in a series of attempts to regain control of the strategic border area with Chad. The joint force stated that the attack began in the early morning along two axes, from Kulbus to the northwest and Sileia to the north. It said its forces destroyed more than 38 combat vehicles, captured another 27 with their equipment and killed the commander of the attacking force along with several other fighters. A military source told Mada Masr that the attackers advanced in large numbers, prompting the joint force to repeat the tactic it had used in previous battles: withdrawing before encircling the advancing force and launching a counterattack. The RSF is now mobilizing fighters in Kulbus, Sileia and Sirba in preparation for another attack on Bir Saliba, the source said. Bir Saliba, about 30 km north of West Darfur capital Geneina, sits on the Sudan-Chad border and serves as a key supply corridor. Control of the area allows forces to monitor cross-border movement, prevent infiltration and flanking maneuvers and secure routes leading north toward Gargira and Tina in North Darfur, where the military maintains major operational bases. The area has changed hands several times since the war began. The military recaptured it on July 11 during a campaign that brought military and allied forces within reach of Geneina. *** Joint force briefly pushes into North Darfur’s Ambro before RSF restores control The joint force of military-allied armed movements launched a surprise attack on RSF positions in the border town of Ambro, North Darfur, on Thursday. A field source in the joint force told Mada Masr their forces captured several combat vehicles before withdrawing from the area later that day. An RSF source, however, said the group had drawn the attackers into an ambush, destroying and capturing several vehicles and killing the commander of the attacking force. The RSF captured Ambro, along the Chadian border, on June 23 as part of an offensive that brought the group deeper into the Zaghawa tribal territory, where the military retains its last positions in Darfur following the fall of Fasher last year. At the time, the RSF fighters launching the assault looted and burned homes, killing and injuring civilians and forcing large numbers of families to flee. *** Military repels major RSF attack on North Kordofan’s Gabra al-Sheikh The RSF launched a large-scale assault on North Kordofan’s Gabra al-Sheikh on Thursday, seeking to retake one of its main logistics hubs in the state weeks after losing it to the military. The military and allied forces repelled the attack after several hours of fighting, according to a military statement and two military sources who spoke to Mada Masr. Gabra al-Sheikh fell to the military in late July as part of a two-day surprise offensive that secured five towns within a 300-square-kilometer area and restored military control over the Saderat Road cutting across North Kordofan. The RSF had used the area to move reinforcements from Darfur via the road and a web of dirt tracks that allowed it to maneuver and redeploy in the region with relative ease. The RSF attacked Gabra al-Sheikh on Thursday with more than 250 combat vehicles, military spokesperson Assem Awad said in a press statement. The military repelled the assault and inflicted heavy losses in personnel and equipment, forcing the attacking forces to withdraw toward Darfur, he said. A member of the Dar Hamar emergency room in West Kordofan told Mada Masr that the RSF had spent the days prior preparing for offensives on Bara and Gabra al-Sheikh. According to a military source, the paramilitary group had amassed forces in the Wudyan, Abu Hadid and Um Surra areas near Gabra al-Sheikh, using the areas’ vegetation as cover to conceal its movements from military aircraft. On Thursday, the fighters moved on the town from three directions and fighting lasted for several hours, involving heavy and light weapons, alongside extensive drone activity, according to a field source affiliated with the military. The attacking force included advanced combat vehicles and weapons, as well as mercenaries of several nationalities, including Libyans and Colombians, the source said. The military captured around 65 combat vehicles and destroyed more than 80 others, the source added. Mohamed Didan, the spokesperson for the military’s special operations forces in West Kordofan, said in a Facebook post that the military was continuing to pursue the remaining RSF fighters of Group 302, led by Ali Balbla, along with RSF-aligned mobilized forces involved in the assault on Gabra al-Sheikh. A senior military officer told Mada Masr that Gabra al-Sheikh was the main operational objective of the RSF’s simultaneous escalation across several fronts in Sudan this week, which they described as a departure from the group’s better-known tactic of rapidly mobilizing forces for concentrated assaults on a single target. Retaking the area would allow the RSF to cut the Saderat Road, put pressure on the military and limit its ability to expand westward, the officer said. They described the fighting in North Kordofan as pivotal to the course of the war, with both sides treating the region as a decisive battlefield. On Thursday, the RSF also attacked Ayyara, located 40 km west of Obeid, North Kordofan’s capital. A field source from the mobilized civilians’ battalions fighting alongside the military said the RSF entered the area with more than 65 combat vehicles, but the attack was repelled and several vehicles were destroyed. *** After clashes inside Kauda, SPLM-N, Otoro fighting spreads to nearby villages Days after the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (Hilu) brought fighting with the Otoro tribe — one of its oldest constituencies — under control inside Kauda, the confrontation has spread to villages on the outskirts of the town, which serves as the movement’s political and military headquarters in South Kordofan. Fighting between the two sides broke out in several areas between Saturday and Monday, according to three sources from villages surrounding Kauda, with SPLM-N forces maintaining a heightened deployment around the town and tightening control over roads leading into it. The villages of Gardud and Hammam saw heavy artillery exchanges, driving dozens of families to flee toward Kubam and Kambra villages, the sources said. Many of these villages sit within corridors linking Kauda to the rural communities the town depends on for food, transport and supplies, according to a military source in SPLM-N factions that split from Hilu. Continued fighting there, the source said, weakens Kauda’s function as an administrative hub, even as the movement’s institutions inside the town itself remain under its control. Last week’s fighting inside Kauda marked the most dangerous escalation yet in a dispute that has been building since 2022, when SPLM-N moved to redraw administrative boundaries in areas under its control and redefine tribal landholdings across the Nuba Mountains. Many Otoro rejected the reform as an encroachment on ancestral land, and resistance eventually spread into the SPLM-N’s own army, where large numbers of Otoro serve. By March, the leadership was treating that resistance as mutiny, and in May it launched military operations in Otoro areas that left more than 60 people dead. Tensions continued to build over the following months, driven by broader Otoro demands for greater representation in the movement’s civilian and military institutions, until they reached SPLM-N’s own seat of power last week. For months now, people have lived under mounting pressure, the three villagers said, with civilian movement and market activity shifting from area to area depending on the security situation. In the words of the source who split from the Hilu faction, it is “a crisis with a moving geography.” Since last week’s escalation, SPLM-N forces deployed around Kauda are treating the area as a tightly controlled security zone, amid fears that fighting could return to the town itself, according to a resident of one of the nearby villages who is familiar with the security situation there. Checkpoints and stricter movement controls have become part of daily life, the source added, and families now weigh travel between villages as a security calculation rather than routine movement. What makes this confrontation harder to resolve, according to a former SPLM-N military source, is who the movement is up against. Unlike confrontations with external rivals, the source said, the SPLM-N faces groups with deep social and historical ties to its areas of influence and intimate knowledge of the local terrain and community networks, meaning military control alone will not be enough to end it. Continued military deployment may force SPLM-N to divert part of its forces and resources toward protecting key centers, roads and strategic sites within its territory, the source added, at a time when it is already under military pressure on other fronts, where it is fighting alongside the RSF against the Sudanese military. This does not necessarily mean the current confrontation threatens the movement’s military control over Kauda, but it does create an internal drain that becomes harder to ignore the longer the crisis continues, according to the source. Restoring calm, though, may be the easier part, according to a former South Kordofan State official who is also a notable of the Nuba peoples. The crisis confronts the movement’s leadership with something more complicated, requiring it to address the relationship between the central authority in Kauda and communities that feel their influence within the movement’s institutions has eroded in recent years. But SPLM-N leadership views the unification of administration and the building of centralized institutions as essential to holding its territories together, a source in SPLM-N told Mada Masr. Even so, the leadership is not blind to the cost. SPLM-N understands that the ongoing confrontation damages the image of the institutions it has built over years, a political source close to the movement said — particularly in Kauda, which stands as a model of local governance the movement has sought to present as an alternative to central state administration. Any long-term shift toward military administration in contested areas risks weakening that model and widening the distance between the institutions and the population, the source added. Both the Nuba notable and an Otoro notable see that continued military operations without addressing the community’s grievances will only produce new rounds of violence, even if the movement manages to impose a temporary calm in one area or another. This could, in the long term, harden into a recurring cycle: clashes in one area, followed by military buildup, followed by displacement and disrupted trade, followed by tension shifting elsewhere, the Nuba notable said. That scenario would put Kauda to a test that measures whether it can preserve its political centrality without that very centrality becoming a permanent source of conflict with everything around it, they added. To deflect such a scenario, the Otoro notable called for local negotiation channels to reopen, with native administrations and community leaders included in any new arrangements over land, security and governance. But while SPLM-N and tribal leaders weigh these long-term questions, people caught in the middle of it are contending with more immediate consequences. Security restrictions have disrupted markets, transportation and services, a field source working in relief operations in South Kordofan told Mada Masr. Residents have come to treat access to certain areas as contingent on the day’s fighting, driving up the cost of securing food and basic services, the source added. Humanitarian organizations, too, are running into obstacles reaching affected areas, the source continued. As the military footprint expands and checkpoints multiply, movement for aid workers and convoys grows more complicated, particularly in a region that relies on limited roads. No comprehensive independent figures yet exist on the scale of humanitarian need generated by the latest round of fighting, the source said, but displacement, market closures and disrupted transportation all point to an impact beyond the areas witnessing direct clashes. *** Kordofan governor in RSF-led govt defects Governor of the Kordofan region and member of the Tasis government’s presidential council Hamad Khalifa announces his defection from the RSF, August 12. Courtesy: Alhadath Alsudani Hamad Khalifa, the governor of the Kordofan region in the RSF-led Tasis government in western Sudan and a member of its presidential council, announced on Wednesday that he is defecting from the RSF, in the latest high-profile departure from the paramilitary group’s political and military camp. In a video interview with Al-Arabiya, Khalifa said he was resigning from his post, disavowing the RSF actions and abuses and calling on its members to return to the state. Khalifa’s departure is significant because of his position within a structure the RSF and its allies have sought to build to present their control over large parts of the country as an alternative political and administrative project, according to a former Sudanese intelligence official. When forming its presidential council in western Sudan last year, the RSF-led Tasis coalition divided Sudan into eight regions and appointed Khalifa governor of Kordofan and a member of the council. Khalifa had kept a low profile for several weeks and stopped attending presidential council meetings, according to a political source close to the Tasis leadership who spoke to Mada Masr. The source said he had left his residence under the pretext of routine administrative tours before announcing his resignation. According to a source close to Khalifa, his decision followed disagreements over the military situation and developments on the ground in his region. The source said he had objected to killings committed by the RSF and to drone attacks on Obeid, after Hemedti failed to heed his calls to rein in his forces. The departure has prompted increased scrutiny of administrative officials and executives working in RSF-controlled areas, according to a source close to Tasis’s political circles who spoke to Mada Masr. The source said regional governors have been instructed to obtain security clearance from the military leadership before moving. Khalifa’s departure follows a series of high-profile defections from the RSF in recent months. Al-Nour “Gubba” Adam, a former RSF commander in North Darfur and Mahamid tribal leader, defected earlier this year, with many of his fighters leaving Darfur with him. In May, former RSF field commander Ali “Savanna” Rizgallah also defected , followed in June by Fares al-Nour, a former close associate of Hemedti who handled sensitive political and diplomatic files. The series of departures do not signal an immediate military collapse of the RSF, a second source in Tasis’s political circles said. The group, they stressed, still has combat formations and the capability to retain control over large areas. For the former intelligence official, the significance of Khalifa’s departure lies in the fact that it adds an administrative dimension to the series of defections that involved military and political figures. Gubba and Savanna showed that field commanders could leave, while Fares al-Nour’s departure showed that Hemedti’s political circle was also susceptible, they said. According to the official, Khalifa’s exit now “puts Tasis’s regional face in question: what does the project look like on the ground if its own representatives begin to withdraw?” That does not amount to a comprehensive fragmentation of the RSF, the former official said. A more accurate description is a gradual fracturing across different levels of loyalty and representation, they added. *** Khartoum targets September for state-led political dialogue, preparations remain contested The intra-Sudanese political dialogue that Burhan has been preparing for months is now being targeted for a September launch, according to three political sources informed of the process and a source close to Burhan who spoke to Mada Masr, as the failure of international mediation in Addis Ababa has prompted a faster push on the domestic track. The government is now working to settle the dialogue’s preparatory arrangements, including who will sit on its preparatory committee, how participants will be selected and what issues will be addressed first, according to the sources. But these arrangements themselves remain contested, with the opposition Sumud coalition arguing that the forces expected to take part in the dialogue must have a say in the preparations, given that they will effectively determine the political process and its outcomes. Burhan had been laying the groundwork for the dialogue for months, consulting political forces, tribal leaders and national figures to build the political backing needed to launch it. But the pace picked up after another attempt to bring Sudan’s rival political camps together broke down in Addis Ababa in late July. The Quintet — comprising the African Union, United Nations, Arab League, European Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development — had convened the consultations to discuss a roadmap for a political process and the formation of a preparatory committee. The meetings failed to produce a joint discussion among the political forces. Instead, the Quintet held bilateral talks with several groups, particularly major blocs allied with the military, while the opposition Sumud coalition and the RSF-led Tasis stayed away. Both groups objected to how the Quintet is managing the mediation process and the selection of participating groups, with Sumud criticizing what it claimed was the Quintet’s insistence on including the former ruling National Congress Party, the Islamist current and affiliated groups. The coalition also objected to the prominent role given to parties aligned with the military-led government. The breakdown in Addis Ababa gave Sudan’s leadership an opening to move more quickly with its own track, a political source involved in the preparations said. September was subsequently set as the target for launching the dialogue inside Sudan. The government has taken cues from the disputes surrounding Addis Ababa. According to the source, the parties involved in the Burhan-led dialogue are seeking a formula that would prevent similar disagreements from derailing the process. For one, the National Congress Party would not take part in the dialogue, according to the source. There are also efforts to accommodate Sumud. More than 30 of its leaders face charges from the Sudanese government alleging that they undermined the constitutional order and rebelled against the state. The political source said efforts are underway to drop the cases, potentially clearing the way for the coalition to participate in the dialogue. But even if the legal issue is resolved, there is no clear agreement on the terms of Sumud’s participation. Bakry al-Jack, the coalition’s spokesperson, told Mada Masr that, in recent months, Sumud held contacts with figures and forces associated with the de facto authorities, but had received neither a formal or informal invitation to join a defined dialogue process. During those contacts, the coalition put forward its own sequencing of the political process, Jack said. Rather than moving directly into dialogue, it wants the process to begin with a cessation of fighting and measures to create a conducive humanitarian and political environment. Its proposal includes a three-month humanitarian truce, humanitarian corridors, guarantees for civilian protection, an end to weapons supplies to the warring parties and a freeze on administrative changes made during the war. The preparatory committee and political dialogue would come afterward. That puts what the political source described as the “pre-dialogue arrangements” at the center of the dispute. The immediate task for authorities now is to settle those arrangements, the political source said, but the substance of what needs to be settled remains contentious. One of the key issues is the composition of the preparatory committee, according to a second source informed of the consultations. The committee would set the format and agenda of the conference and communicate with political and civil forces and establish the rules for participation. Discussions are still focused on its size and selection, including whether the main political blocs should be represented equally or whether other civilian and community-based forces should be brought in. The stakes are high because the committee would, in practice, determine who gets a seat at the dialogue table. According to Jack, Sumud argues that the arrangements for the dialogue, including the committee formation, should themselves be negotiated, rather than determined in advance and presented to the participating forces as a finished process. That is significant because the government’s “pre-dialogue arrangements” already include a work plan, an initial outline of the agenda, according to the source close to Burhan, even though the preparatory committee would later be tasked with organizing and developing it. The agenda is contentious in part because the government and war opponents do not share the same starting point. Burhan sees the dialogue as a vehicle for rebuilding state institutions and setting the terms for the next phase, with the military-led authorities retaining control over the process. Forces opposed to the war, by contrast, want the fighting to end and a political and humanitarian environment to be established before questions about political power and the future shape of the state are taken up. The government is seeking to move toward its end point in stages, rather than convening a single, unwieldy conference expected to settle every issue at once, a third political source said. The proposed process would begin with a preparatory phase, followed by political sessions, and then discussions on the transitional period and rebuilding state institutions. The preparatory committee would determine how issues are prioritized and when they are brought into the process, the source said. That makes both the committee’s composition and the work plan already taking shape consequential for parties looking to secure a place in the process. If the initial outline sets the direction of the dialogue, the committee could have limited room to alter it, and whoever controls its membership will ultimately have a say in determining which issues receive priority. Excluding a political force from the preparatory phase thus would effectively exclude it from shaping the rules of the dialogue and eventually its outcomes. Contacts will continue in the coming period as the parties try to settle the formula before September, with both the participant list and the preparatory committee still unresolved, according to the three political sources. *** Back-to-back Sudanese visits to Juba in mutual push to contain border, Abyei tensions Sudanese Defense Minister Hassan Kabron and his South Sudanese counterpart Chol Thon Balok meet at the Ministry of Defence and Veterans Affairs headquarters in Juba, August 10. Courtesy: The Sudanese Defense Ministry A month of high-level maneuvering around Khartoum-Juba relations continued this week, with two back-to-back visits to the South Sudanese capital — Sudanese Defense Minister Hassan Kabron on Sunday, followed a day later by Darfur Governor Minni Arko Minnawi. Kabron led a senior military and security delegation into talks with his South Sudanese counterpart. The next day, Minnawi held meetings with Tut Gatluak, the security affairs advisor to President Salva Kiir. The shared border and the armed groups moving across it dominated both sets of talks, alongside the disputed Abyei territory and the protection of oil interests on both sides of the border. The flurry of activity follows South Sudan’s mid-July announcement that stirred formal protest in Khartoum: Abyei, unresolved between the two states since the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement, would be folded into the electoral districts for the country’s first general elections, scheduled for December. Simultaneously, Sudan’s military has been pushing deeper into Kordofan — the oil-rich region bordering South Sudan that carries the infrastructure piping South Sudanese oil through Sudan for export — with vows to keep advancing toward Darfur. The two delegations’ visits to Juba came as an attempt to reopen a direct channel with Sudan’s military leadership, a Sudanese diplomatic source said, at a moment when South Sudan’s approaching political and electoral milestones make it all the more important for Juba to keep its northern border out of the escalation. That border carries particular weight given the fighting underway in Sudan, where the military is trying to sever the RSF’s supply lines from Ethiopia, Libya and Chad — potentially leaving South Sudan’s northern border as the RSF’s last remaining resupply route, according to the source. The visits also pave the way for Burhan’s own trip to Juba soon, the source added. In a visit to Khartoum in late July, Gatluak delivered a written message from Kiir to Burhan inviting him to a bilateral summit in Juba in the coming weeks, with the agenda covering a range of unresolved issues — Abyei, border demarcation and stalled security and economic arrangements among them, according to a Sudanese diplomatic source who spoke to Mada Masr at the time Border control was the focus of Kabron’s own talks in Juba, including blocking the movement of armed groups, protecting oil facilities and pipelines and discussing temporary security arrangements to contain tensions around Abyei, according to a South Sudanese source informed of the visit. Minnawi’s talks covered much the same topics. A Sudanese diplomatic source informed of the trip told Mada Masr that the visit focused on the Abyei file, the war’s impact on the Sudan-South Sudan border and the movement of armed forces and groups across it. The meeting also discussed political and security contacts with South Sudanese officials, the source added, at a moment when Juba’s role in southern and western Sudan’s security arrangements is growing. Khartoum can treat Abyei as an open negotiating issue, a former senior Sudanese diplomat familiar with the file said. But it struggles with South Sudanese measures that create new administrative and political facts on the ground in the disputed area — one of the factors, the diplomat added, that has accelerated security contacts between the two countries. The concern is that political disputes could turn into friction on the ground, particularly given the area’s history of tension between the Ngok Dinka and the Misseria tribes, seasonal herder movements across the border and fragile security arrangements. Sensitivities in Abyei have doubled since the Sudan war broke out, an official in the territory said. Large numbers of displaced people have flowed into the area, straining resources, services and traditional grazing routes, while the area itself has grown more exposed to the fallout of military operations on the Sudanese side of the border. The UN’s interim security force for Abyei, UNISFA, continues to monitor military movements and local tensions, the source said. “The presence of armed forces and armed groups around Abyei adds to the complexity,” the official said. “The further the Sudanese war extends south and west, the more important these border areas become as movement and supply lines. Juba is trying to stop its border with Sudan from turning into an open corridor for fighters and weapons.” Oil is central to these calculations. South Sudan relies almost entirely on Sudanese infrastructure to move its crude through Sudanese territory to Red Sea ports. Khartoum, in turn, collects transit fees that count among the few revenue sources it has left amid the war. That makes the Heglig oil fields, pipelines and related facilities in West Kordofan, bordering Abyei, a shared national security concern. Any major disruption to production or transport areas would carry a direct cost for Juba’s economy and for public finances in Khartoum. Juba is keen to keep the political dispute over Abyei separate from the economic interests tied to oil, a South Sudanese official informed of the file said. The South Sudanese government recognizes a major security escalation on the border would hurt both sides. Kiir’s government still faces domestic pressure on the issue, though, from political forces and local communities who feel the Abyei file has been left hanging too long and want steps taken to affirm the territory’s ties to South Sudan, according to the source. A senior South Sudanese government official described Gatluak’s visit to Khartoum and Kabron’s visit to Juba as reflecting both sides’ wish to build a more regular security channel. Ugandan contacts with Khartoum over South Sudan in recent weeks add a regional layer to these arrangements, the official said. Kampala’s involvement carries particular weight given its place in the web of security and political relationships surrounding the Sudanese war, and its direct ties to the South Sudan file. The old bilateral mechanisms can no longer keep pace with the new realities Sudan’s war has created, another Sudanese diplomat said, and the two states are now seeking direct lines of contact between their military and security bodies instead. The real test of these contacts, the diplomat added, will come in Abyei more than in any other file, since any friction there could quickly escalate into a crisis between the two states, especially with South Sudan’s elections drawing near. *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . items.title: Des vivres et non-vivres aux victimes des inondations
items.description: Tabligbo, 14 août (ATOP) – Soixante-cinq ménages victimes des inondations des pluies diluviennes du 28 juin dernier dans les localités de Essè-Godjin, Akladjénou, Atakpamédé et de Gboto-Klohomé dans la commune Yoto 3 ont bénéficié de kits de vivres et non-vivres, le jeudi 13 août dans leurs localités respectives. Chaque ménage a reçu un kit composé notamment d’un sac de riz de 25kg, d’un bidon d’huile de 3 litres, des ustensiles de cuisine. Deux seaux en plastique, deux couvertures épaisses de deux places, deux nattes, cinq pièces de savons, deux sacs de conditionnement. L’ONG Plan international-Togo, à travers cette action, entend apporter un soutien aux ménages touchés. Il s’agit aussi de renforcer leur capacité à faire face aux difficultés engendrées par le sinistre. Un lot des kits A l’occasion, l’assistance a été sensibilisée sur la gestion des risques liées aux catastrophes et la politique de sauvegarde de Plan international Togo. Les échanges ont permis de rappeler aux bénéficiaires les comportements à adopter face aux risques et les mécanismes de protection mis en place par l’organisation. Dans le souci de renforcer la prise en compte des préoccupations des bénéficiaires, un comité de veille de trois membres a été mis en place. Il aura notamment pour mission de recueillir les plaintes et préoccupations liées à l’intervention. Le directeur de la mise en œuvre des programmes de Plan international Togo, Soba Palakeyém a expliqué la stratégie mise en place par l’organisation pour répondre aux besoins des victimes. Il a également appelé les populations à davantage de prudence dans le choix des sites de construction, notamment en évitant les zones marécageuses et les lits des cours d’eau. Le coordinateur des programmes de Plan international dans la région Maritime et des Plateaux, Tsigbé Kodjo a précisé que les kits distribués constituent un premier secours en attendant la mobilisation d’autres moyens pour répondre durablement aux besoins des ménages affectés. Il les a invités à prendre soin des kits. Les bénéficiaires ont exprimé leur remerciement aux donateurs pour cette action humanitaire et de générosité. La remise s’est déroulée en présence des autorités locales, des chefs de services, des représentants de l’Agence nationale de la protection civile (ANPC) et du ministère en charge des Solidarités ainsi que des responsables des forces de défense et de sécurité. ATOP/SAK/MG/BV
